scenario: Most of today's embodied AI papers ask the same question: how a general robot model gets from demos to stable deployment. Kimodo-Policy and SWAM change the pretraining base: the first freezes a motion generator as its backbone, and the second pretrains a world action model on large-scale video and human demonstrations and finds that caption detail affects control. DASH takes the slow backbone off the control loop, and CTR retimes bimanual demonstrations to remove false dependencies that policies learn from demonstration order. Tactile sensors can stand in for wrist cameras on contact-rich tasks, and AnchorQ refines frozen policies with a small set of meaningful candidate actions.

papers.title: Practice Makes Precise: At CoRL, NVIDIA and Partners Reveal How Robots Rehearse Delicate Work in Simulation
papers.abstract: Simulation, which has long been the proving ground for robots learning to walk, roll and hop, is now helping researchers teach robots tasks that require a finer touch: aligning gears, connecting cables and assembling small components.  The shift from locomotion to manipulation is taking center stage at this week’s Conference on Robot Learning (CoRL) in […]
papers.summary: Simulation has long been where robots learn to walk, and NVIDIA now wants to use it for fine work such as aligning gears and connecting cables, where the parts are millimeter-scale and training each task separately burns GPU time without reaching high success. Among the work it presented at CoRL, AlphaNIST shows the progress best: a single policy learns every task on the NIST assembly board and receives only a success-or-failure signal during training. It reaches more than 98% training success, compared with 81% when each task gets its own policy, and uses roughly 39 times less GPU time. The sampling method behind it is plain: it favors tasks the policy succeeds at about half the time, which concentrates practice on skills still being learned. ==Training resources belong on what is only half learned==, which is what recommender engineers do when they weight hard samples.

papers.title: Learn the Task, Not the Schedule: Reducing Spurious Cross-Arm Coupling in Bimanual Imitation Learning
papers.authors: Shuyuan Hu, Deng-Ke Wu, Yifan Jin, Qianhang Luo, Mingchen Ju, Kai Ye, Bo Zhao
papers.abstract: A bimanual demonstration specifies both what the robot should do and one particular schedule for when each arm should act. Standard imitation learning does not distinguish task-required cross-arm constraints from incidental scheduling choices, and may therefore exploit opposite-arm progress as a shortcut cue, creating spurious cross-arm coupling even where relative timing is irrelevant for the current task phase. We introduce Constraint-preserving Temporal Recombination (CTR), a training-time data intervention that preserves recorded arm-local sensorimotor content while retiming the corresponding segments to realize admissible schedules that preserve task-required cross-arm constraints. We use CTR to train Diffusion Policy, Action Chunking with Transformers, and $\pi_{0.5}$, and evaluate them on four simulated and four real-robot tasks. Across six real-robot bimanual progress-state initializations, CTR raises worst-state success from 56% for the strongest non-CTR schedule mixture to 76%. With $\pi_{0.5}$ on an Independent task, a 4 s pause transfers 2.56 s of delay to the opposite arm under the Concurrent schedule distribution, but only 0.25 s with CTR. On real robots, CTR violates task constraints in only 0--4% of trials, versus 36--98% for narrow-schedule baselines. Code will be released at https://github.com/MINT-SJTU/CTR.
papers.summary: In two-armed robot demonstrations, which hand moves first is often just the operator's habit, yet imitation learning cannot separate the orderings a task requires from the ones that happened by chance, so when one arm is paused the other waits too. The authors audited four public bimanual datasets and found that tasks whose order could change rarely include more than one recorded order, and more data with the same order does not fix this. CTR cuts each arm's recording into segments and retimes them while keeping the required orderings, such as opening a drawer before placing something inside, with no new data collection. On a real robot, pausing one arm for 4 seconds costs the other arm 2.56 extra seconds under a policy trained only on concurrent-start data, and only 0.25 seconds with CTR. ==Coincidences in demonstration order get learned as signal==, and spurious correlations from exposure order in recommenders arise the same way.

papers.title: Kimodo-Policy: Learning Kinematic Action Models for Humanoid Loco-Manipulation
papers.authors: Yunheng Wang, Jiaxi Zhang, Wei Lu, Yuetong Fang, Taowen Wang, Yixiao Feng, Shuning Zhang, Junzhe Xu, Yichi Wang, Zizhao Yuan, Kailun Huang, Lusong Li, Mingqian Zhou, Zecui Zeng, Renjing Xu
papers.abstract: Humanoid loco-manipulation requires continuous coordination of high-dimensional whole-body motion to realize task objectives. While vision-language-action models and world action models transfer semantic and visual-dynamics priors to robot control, these priors do not necessarily capture the structure of robot motion. We introduce Kinematic Action Models (KAMs), a paradigm that treats whole-body motion as a direct pretraining target and uses a pretrained motion generator as the primary action-generation backbone. KAMs ground learned temporal and cross-body coordination priors through task conditioning, visual observations, and execution feedback. We present Kimodo-Policy as an initial instantiation, combining a frozen Kimodo text-to-motion backbone with lightweight ControlNet-based visual conditioning. A root-body-hand hierarchy coordinates locomotion and manipulation, while motion-history conditioning and repeated action-chunk prediction bridge motion synthesis and closed-loop control. Following large-scale loco-manipulation pretraining, the policy achieves the highest overall success among compared policies on multi-task HumanoidArena (72.14%), competitive performance on SIMPLE, and 60% mean success across eight real-world tasks, with 678M parameters (92M trainable). Ablations support the contribution of the pretrained motion backbone. Together, these results provide initial evidence for motion generation as a complementary foundation for humanoid action learning.
papers.summary: When a humanoid walks while picking things up, its torso, arms and legs must coordinate continuously, yet existing vision-language-action and world action models inherit semantics and visual dynamics from pretraining and still have to learn body coordination downstream. This paper changes the pretraining target: it takes a text-to-motion model for the whole body as a frozen backbone and trains only small branches that feed in camera images, plus hand control. With the same structure randomly initialized and then trained, success on object-interaction tasks falls from 51.67% to 18.33%, which indicates that the inherited motion structure does help. On a real robot the mean success across eight tasks is 60%, while the lead on simulated leaderboards is small. ==With motion as the pretraining target, downstream training only has to connect the images==, the same practice as freezing a pretrained model and training only an adapter layer in recommenders.

papers.title: SimDuoReal: Object-Centric Bimanual Policy for Emergent Dexterity
papers.authors: Qiyang Yan, Yulin Liu, Akash Sharma, Haozhi Qi, Guanya Shi, C. Karen Liu
papers.abstract: Bimanual dexterous manipulation requires coordinated arm and hand control, yet specifying such coordination manually is challenging and often task-specific. In this work, we explore whether complex bimanual dexterity can emerge from a simple object-centric learning objective. We train reinforcement learning policies under a shared object-centric reward, varying their training environments rather than tuning separate rewards for each behavior. We find that the policies discover pre-grasp manipulation, grasping and regrasping, in-hand adjustment and handover to reach object-pose goals without hand-designed motion sequences. We then refine the experts on transition states and use DAgger and reinforcement learning to distill them into a single policy that composes these behaviors for diverse bimanual tasks. On real hardware, the same policy succeeds in 61 of 80 trials (76.3\%) across four tasks with unseen objects and no task-specific fine-tuning. In simulated barcode scanning, our policy achieves 85.0\% success, compared with 60.4\% for two single-arm policies without handover. These results suggest that this objective provides a simple and scalable interface for learning general bimanual dexterity, shifting the burden from manually designing robot coordination to specifying what should happen to the object.
papers.summary: The hard part of making two dexterous hands cooperate is specifying which hand moves and when to pass the object, and past work mostly wrote rewards or skill sequences for each behavior, which had to be redone for each new task. This paper tries another route: the reward is written only around the object, checking whether it reached the goal pose and whether the right hand touches it, and only the training environment changes. For example, when the goal sits in the other hand's workspace, the object cannot get there without a handover, and grasping, in-hand adjustment and handover were all trained this way. Three expert policies are then distilled into one, which reaches 76.3% success on four real-robot tasks with unseen objects and no task-specific tuning. In simulated barcode scanning it reaches 85.0%, while two single-arm policies without handover reach 60.4%. ==The engineering moves from writing rewards to designing the training distribution==, the same trade-off recommender engineers face when tuning sample distributions.

papers.title: Tactile Sensors Are an Effective Substitute for Wrist Cameras in Contact-Rich or Occluded Manipulation
papers.authors: Aijia Yang, Arsh Tangri, Sergey Zakharov, Krishna Murthy Jatavallabhula
papers.abstract: Learned manipulation policies often rely on wrist-mounted cameras for close-range visual feedback that complements external views of the workspace. However, contact-rich manipulation requires establishing and maintaining contacts that can remain hidden even from wrist cameras. Tactile sensors mounted on fingers can reliably and directly measure contact, without needing visual access. In this work, we show that this feedback enables policies to recover the performance advantage of wrist cameras using scene and egocentric vision together with touch. Our approach incorporates two low-cost tactile arrays into a visuotactile ACT policy, without wrist images during training or deployment. We evaluate six real-world task families spanning placement, insertion, occluded retrieval, and sustained-contact tool use. On three contact-rich tasks, we independently vary wrist-camera and tactile availability while keeping the demonstrations, policy architecture, and optimization settings fixed. Adding wrist cameras improves success by 18.3-28.3 percentage points over vision without wrist images. Adding tactile sensing instead improves success by 31.7-60.0 percentage points and yields higher observed success than vision-only policies with wrist cameras on all three tasks, with significant advantages on two under Holm-corrected tests. These results support finger-mounted tactile sensing as an effective alternative to wrist cameras in the evaluated contact-rich settings.
papers.summary: Wrist cameras are nearly standard for robot-arm policies, yet once the fingers close, the camera cannot see the actual point of contact. Earlier work showed that touch helps but did not answer whether it can directly replace the wrist camera. The authors mount two low-cost tactile arrays on the inner gripper surfaces and feed the readings into the same ACT policy as two extra images, with demonstrations and training settings unchanged. On three contact-rich tasks, retrieving an object, inserting a plug and wiping a whiteboard, the policy with touch and no wrist camera beats the vision-only policy with a wrist camera every time. The difference is significant on two tasks, with 81.7% against 50.0% for retrieval from an opaque bag. Using both inputs does not reliably help further. ==Vision brings the hand to contact, and the state after contact depends on touch==, and when adding ranking features, signals that cover a blind spot are worth the most too.

papers.title: Compass 1: Towards Open-World and Persistent Embodied Navigation from Monocular RGB Videos
papers.authors: Hai Zhang, Siqi Liang, Yanjun Guo, Shoufeng Zhang, Yunhao Wang, Hangyu Du, Haoguang Mai, Hongchen Li, Jiazhi Yang, Jialong Zeng, Yu Hu, Chen Chen, Gangcheng Jiang, Zishun Zhuo, Lirui Zhao, Zhigang Li, Yu Qiao, Zhenjie Yang, Fu Zhang, Hongyang Li
papers.abstract: Embodied navigation requires agents to achieve persistent spatial awareness and long-horizon execution stability in open-world environments. However, existing navigation architectures struggle to sustain both capabilities, remaining effective only over a handful of recent frames. We present Compass 1, the first embodied navigation foundation model to unify language understanding and video generation while enabling memory backtracking through nearly 2mins of visual history. Without altering the underlying architecture, we introduce History Representation, which integrates sparse visual keyframes with an explicit History Representation Map to preserve long-term spatiotemporal context. To effectively leverage this history, we further introduce History Utilization, a structured VQA supervision protocol comprising three categories: task-stage grounding, exploration consistency, and spatiotemporal target retrieval, enabling map-grounded reasoning and stable persistent long-horizon navigation. To fuel this system, we establish a complete annotation pipeline for monocular RGB videos and open-source a massive dataset featuring over 500 hours of high-quality real-world interactions and over 2,000 hours of annotated web videos. Trained mainly on the distribution of 1m height camera, Compass 1 generalizes seamlessly across diverse embodiments and scenarios, ranging from indoor environments to pedestrian-dense streets, spanning wheeled robot at 0.35m, quadruped dog at 0.5m, humanoid at 0.85m, and aerial drone at 1.5m. Compass 1achieves a dominant overall success rate of 79.4% across open-world evaluations, compared to 17.8% for the strongest baseline. It demonstrates exceptional zero-shot execution exceeding 90% on foundational tasks, a 250% boost in exploration, and an unparalleled leap from 0% to 58% in challenging persistent history backtracking.
papers.summary: Navigation models usually make use of only the last few frames, so returning to a target that left view long ago is nearly impossible, feeding in every past frame hurts attention quality and costs heavy compute, and sampling frames at a fixed interval loses information. Compass 1 draws the path traveled as a 2D map, marks it with keyframe numbers and headings, and feeds it with sparse keyframes as ordinary images, leaving the model architecture unchanged. The map alone does nothing because the backbone ignores it, so training adds question-and-answer supervision that asks which frame shows the target and which direction to go now. Overall success in real-world scenes is 79.4%, against 17.8% for the strongest baseline. On the hardest task of returning to an unseen target, every baseline fails and Compass 1 reaches 58%. ==History has to be compressed, and supervision has to force the model to use it==, which is also the sticking point in long-term behavior sequence modeling.

papers.title: Gemini Robotics 2.5 accelerates real-world general dexterity
papers.abstract: Our most capable vision-language-action model enhances robot dexterity, reliability, and safety
papers.summary: General-purpose robot policies can already follow instructions and do many things, but reaching deployment-level reliability remains hard. DeepMind has released Gemini Robotics 2.5 and calls it its most capable vision-language-action model, a class of model that takes images, robot state and text instructions and directly outputs the next chunk of actions. The company places the selling points of this upgrade on better dexterity, reliability and safety, and the headline stresses general dexterity in the real world. Other papers in this track today are working on the same gap, for example using touch to cover contact that cameras cannot see and reinforcement learning to make a frozen general policy more reliable. ==Putting reliability and safety in the headline shifts the contest toward deployment==, the same concern behind not judging online systems by offline metrics alone.

papers.title: SWAM: Scaling World Action Models with Cross-Modal Alignment
papers.authors: Yu Zhou, Xinyuan Xia, Xuankun Yang, Yinghao Yang, Wendi Chen, Bowen Liu, Jianhan Ma, Weicheng Duan, Jun Lv, Cewu Lu, Yanwei Li
papers.abstract: World action models jointly predict video and actions conditioned on language. Existing studies focus primarily on architectures and training mechanisms, typically treating language-video alignment acquired through video pretraining as an established foundation. However, introducing action learning may impair this alignment. Principled guidance on data and supervision design for maintaining language-video alignment during action learning remains limited. To investigate this, we curate a pool of approximately 47,000 hours of general videos, egocentric videos, UMI demonstrations, and robot demonstrations. Building on this, we systematically study how language-video supervision, language-video-action supervision, and the joint use of these two forms affect WAM performance. In particular, we examine how language annotation quality affects pretrained language-video capabilities, and how action supervision from UMI and robot demonstrations extends these capabilities to language-video-action modeling. To better scale the model, we further conduct detailed studies on joint training recipe and model architecture. Under a fixed training budget, mixing egocentric videos and UMI demonstrations improves control generalization. Model architecture affects how effectively these experiences are used, while scaling pretraining under the selected configuration brings further gains. The resulting recipe, post-trained on RoboTwin Clean demonstrations only, achieves success rates of 88.10% and 61.56% under Easy (Clean-to-Clean) and Hard (Clean-to-Random) conditions, respectively. Our model achieves 40.00% SR across three real-world tasks, compared with 23.33% for the strongest baseline, indicating better generalization under unseen conditions. We release the curated data, training code, and model weights.
papers.summary: World action models predict future video and robot actions together and usually start from video pretraining, and existing work assumes the text-to-image correspondence learned there survives action training, while guidance on how to organize data and annotation is limited. This paper runs item-by-item comparisons on about 47,000 hours of general video, first-person video, handheld gripper demonstrations and robot data, and finds that caption quality directly affects control. With the same training budget, rewriting subtask captions from one verb-object phrase into a step-by-step account and adding scene and lighting details raises success from 47.20% to 55.04% on simulated tasks with changed backgrounds and lighting. Training on a mix of first-person video and handheld gripper demonstrations also beats using either one alone. ==More detailed captions end up as better actions==, so anyone doing multimodal pretraining should audit annotations early.

papers.title: Decoupled Asynchronous System for Humanoids (DASH): Latency-Agnostic Scaling of Vision-Language-Action Models for Humanoid Manipulation
papers.authors: Bingzhang Wang, Nathan Zhao, Jialeng Ni, Jiajin Zheng, Yin Zhang, Kehua Chen, Jian Yao
papers.abstract: Vision-language-action (VLA) models pair a vision-language backbone with an action head, but in closed-loop control the backbone sits on the control-critical path: while it computes, the robot keeps moving, so each executed action is conditioned on an increasingly stale observation. A larger backbone therefore directly blocks reactivity, especially in humanoid dexterous manipulation. We present DASH, a Decoupled Asynchronous System for Humanoids that removes this coupling. DASH splits the policy into a slow vision-language model (System 2) and a fast flow-matching action head (System 1) that run as concurrent processes over the LCM communication protocol, so the control rate is set by the action head alone, independent of backbone size. The action head fuses stale semantics from a frozen backbone with fresh vision from its own ResNet encoder, desynchronized training exposes it to the staleness it meets at deployment, and an adaptive temporal aggregator aligns overlapping action chunks under variable inference latency. On an asynchronous RoboTwin benchmark that charges inference latency in simulated time, DASH holds 20 Hz control rate from 0.8B to 8B backbones while the synchronous rate falls from 9.7 to 4.1 Hz, with higher success at every size. On a real humanoid with dexterous hands, DASH achieves clearly higher pick-and-place success than the synchronous pipeline.
papers.summary: The backbone of a vision-language-action model is slow and the robot does not stop to wait, so actions are computed from stale images, the problem grows with backbone size, and deployments settle for small backbones. DASH splits the slow backbone and the fast action head into concurrent processes: the action head reads the backbone's latest semantic output and combines it with fresh image features from its own vision encoder, so the action head alone sets the control rate. From the smallest backbone to the largest, the control rate holds at 20 Hz, while the synchronous setup falls from 9.7 Hz to 4.1 Hz. Splitting alone is not enough: the asynchronous version trained on aligned data is no better than synchronous, and success exceeds synchronous only when training deliberately pairs the action head with old semantic features and new images. ==Time offsets in training samples must match production==, just as training and serving feature freshness must match in recommenders.

papers.title: Sample-Efficient Reinforcement Learning for Policy Improvement via Flow-Reversed Action Anchors
papers.authors: Carl Qi, Weijun Dong, Xiaojie Wang, Peiyi Chen, Rahul Sajnani, Mingyuan Zhang, Amy Zhang, Jose Barreiros, Manikantan Nambi, Lillian J. Ratliff, Dylan Randle
papers.abstract: Generalist robot policies offer strong behavioral priors, but achieving deployment-level reliability and throughput remains difficult. Reinforcement learning (RL) can improve these policies, yet its effectiveness is constrained by the cost of online interaction. Existing methods adapt frozen flow-matching policies by treating noise space as a continuous action space. We show that this behaviorally unstructured space makes exploration inefficient, often preventing these methods from extracting meaningful learning signals on challenging tasks. We introduce AnchorQ, which enables coarse-to-fine policy improvement through a structured, refinable latent action representation. At each decision step, AnchorQ uses flow reversal to map reference behaviors to state-conditioned latent anchors, samples local particles around those anchors, and applies value-guided sampling to explore promising refinements. Our analysis shows that anchors reduce identification complexity at the cost of support bias; particle refinement trades this bias against action-class complexity; and critic accuracy determines the reliability of KL-regularized, value-guided selection. Across simulated and real-world manipulation tasks, AnchorQ outperforms state-of-the-art post-training baselines in sample efficiency, delivering a 37% improvement in real-world success rate and 97% higher simulated task throughput under the same interaction budget. Additional visualizations are available on our website https://anchorq-rl.com/.
papers.summary: A common way to improve a frozen general robot policy on a specific task is to use reinforcement learning to search the initial noise it generates actions from. But directions in noise space have no regular link to actions and online interaction is costly, so exploration is inefficient. AnchorQ first maps coarse motions such as moves in six directions back into noise, which gives a small set of meaningful candidates at each step (the paper calls them anchors), then samples refinements near them, and a value network picks the highest-scoring one. With the same 500,000 interaction steps, a simulated task suite reaches 95.5% success, against 48.3% for DSRL, which searches the noise directly. On a real robot with a small interaction budget, it also beats DSRL on all three tasks. ==Marking meaningful candidates first and then refining locally== reads like the retrieve-then-rerank pattern in search, and it saves far more than blind search in a continuous space when the exploration budget is tight.
